overview.title: Language Overview
overview.summary: High-performance object-oriented scripting language fusing Pythonic syntax with native C++23 speed and WebAssembly execution.

sections.title: What is Sardine?
sections.content:
Sardine is a modern, dynamically-typed, object-oriented programming language engineered in C++23. It brings together the syntactic clarity of Python and the deterministic execution speed, memory safety, and thread predictability of native systems code.

The entire language pipeline compiles cleanly to native binaries and WebAssembly, enabling interactive execution, step-by-step AST inspection, and educational visualization directly inside the browser.

sections.title: Architecture Pipeline
rows: Tokenizes raw character streams and filters whitespace/comments.
Constructs a typed Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) using operator precedence.
Executes AST nodes with scoped Context Maps and hierarchical Symbol Tables.
Executes compilation and sandboxed interpretation safely in browser threads.

# Dynamic iteration with step

sections.title: Self-Hosted Standard Library
sections.content: A significant portion of Sardine's standard library (including math, linear algebra, statistics, and random number generation) is written directly in Sardine itself, demonstrating both the expressive power and performance of the language engine.

quickstart.title: Quickstart & Tooling
quickstart.summary: Compile, run scripts from the command line, use the interactive REPL, and leverage telemetry profiling tools.

sections.title: Execution Modes
sections.content:
Sardine can be executed in three primary modes:
1. **CLI Script Runner**: Pass a `.sad` script file directly to the executable.
2. **Interactive Shell (REPL)**: Launch `./build/sardine` without arguments to enter an interactive session where commands are executed line-by-line.
3. **Web Playground**: Open the integrated WebAssembly playground to run code, debug step-by-step, and inspect AST hierarchies in real time.

sections.title: CLI Commands
sections.content:
# Launch interactive REPL
./build/sardine

# Execute a script file
./build/sardine samples/main.sad

# Run with unlimited iterations and container sizes
./build/sardine samples/main.sad --unbounded

# Run with educational AST output
./build/sardine samples/main.sad --edu

sections.title: Command-Line Flags

Serializes educational compiler diagnostics and tokens as structured JSON.

sections.title: Web Sandbox Security
sections.content: In the WebAssembly environment, code runs inside a dedicated Web Worker thread with SharedArrayBuffer communication. Infinite loops are intercepted by strict iteration caps (100,000 iterations default) to keep your browser responsive.

variables.title: Variables & Dynamic Typing
variables.summary: Dynamically typed variable declarations, lexical scoping, reassignment, and naming rules.

sections.title: Dynamic Variable Assignment
sections.content:
In Sardine, variables are dynamically typed and declared upon their first assignment using the `=` operator. There is no need for explicit type annotations or `let`/`var` keywords.

Variable identifiers can consist of uppercase and lowercase ASCII letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or match a reserved language keyword.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
sections.content:
identifier = expression
identifier = new_value  # Can change types dynamically

sections.title: Declaring & Reassigning Variables
sections.code:
# Simple assignment
count = 10
ratio = 3.14159
language = "Sardine"
is_ready = True

show("Initial values:", count, ratio, language, is_ready)

# Dynamic type reassignment
item = 42
show("item as Integer:", item, "| type:", type(item))

item = "Now I am a String"
show("item as String:", item, "| type:", type(item))

item = [1, 2, 3]
show("item as List:", item, "| type:", type(item))

sections.title: Lexical Scope Resolution
sections.content: Sardine scopes variables lexically. When accessing a variable, the runtime searches the local Symbol Table first, then parent function closures, and finally the global Symbol Table.

primitives.title: Primitive Types & Null
primitives.summary: Core primitive literals including Integers, Floats, Booleans, Null sentinels, and type converter functions.

sections.title: Primitive Data System
sections.content:
Sardine features five primary primitive types:
* **Integer**: 64-bit signed two's-complement integer (`long long`). Supports arbitrary mathematical operations and bit shifts.
* **Float**: 64-bit IEEE 754 double precision floating-point number.
* **Boolean**: Logical values represented by `True` and `False` (mapped internally to 1 and 0).
* **Null**: Sentinel representing the absence of a value. Accessible via any of the aliases `Null`, `None`, or `null`.
* **Type Inspection**: Use `type(x)` to retrieve the type name string.

sections.content:

Float(val)     # Casts number or numeric string to Float

String(val)    # Converts any value to its string representation
type(val)      # Returns type string, e.g. "Integer", "Float", "Null"

sections.title: Truthiness of Null
sections.content: `Null`, `None`, and `null` evaluate to falsy in conditional statements (`when`, `orwhen`). In comparisons, `Null` only equals itself.

strings.title: Strings & Formatted F-Strings
strings.summary: Immutable character sequences, string concatenation, repetition, indexing, and expression interpolation via F-strings.

sections.title: String Syntax & Interpolation
sections.content:
Strings in Sardine are immutable character sequences surrounded by double quotes `"..."`. They support standard escape characters (`\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\`).

**Formatted Strings (F-strings)** are prefixed with `$`, e.g. `$"Hello {name}"`. Any valid Sardine expression can be embedded inside `{}` curly braces and will be evaluated and stringified at runtime.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
sections.content:
str = "Hello, World!"
fstr = $"Calculated value: {2 * 21}"

# Operators
merged = str1 + str2   # Concatenation
repeat = "Ha" * 3      # Repetition -> "HaHaHa"
char = str[0]          # 0-based character indexing

sections.title: String Expressions & Interpolation
sections.code:
# Basic strings and operators
s1 = "Mission"
s2 = "Sardine"
full = s1 + " " + s2
show("Concatenation:", full)

show(accent)

# Indexing
word = "Rocket"
show("First char:", word[0])
show("Third char:", word[2])

# F-strings (Expression Interpolation)
user = "Souvik"
score = 98.5
rank = 1

message = $"Player {user} ranked #{rank} with a score of {score}! High score? {score > 90}"
show(message)

# Expressions inside F-strings
x = 15
y = 25
show($"Math in f-string: {x} + {y} = {x + y}, {x} * {y} = {x * y}")

sections.title: String Interning Optimization
sections.content: Sardine's C++23 runtime engine employs pointer-keyed string interning for variable identifiers and dictionary keys, allowing symbol table lookups to run in O(1) time without character-by-character comparisons.

unpacking.title: Multiple Assignment & Unpacking
unpacking.summary: Destructure lists, strings, and multi-value function yields into distinct variables in a single statement.

sections.title: Unpacking Mechanics
sections.content:
Sardine supports multi-target assignment and sequence unpacking. When assigning a list, string, or multiple-yield function to a comma-separated list of identifiers on the left-hand side, Sardine binds each element positionally.

If the count of LHS variables does not match the size of the RHS iterable, a `RunTimeError` is raised.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
sections.content:
# List unpacking
a, b, c = [1, 2, 3]

# String unpacking
x, y = "AB"

# Multi-value function return unpacking
first, second = get_pair()

sections.title: Destructuring Sequences & Returns
sections.code:
# 1. List Unpacking
x, y, z = [10, 20, 30]
show("x:", x, "y:", y, "z:", z)

# 2. String Unpacking
char1, char2, char3 = "SAD"
show("Chars:", char1, char2, char3)

# 3. Function Multi-Yield Unpacking
method get_user_coordinates() {
    latitude = 40.7128
    longitude = -74.0060
    altitude = 10
    yield latitude, longitude, altitude
}

lat, lon, alt = get_user_coordinates()
show("Coordinates:")
show("  Latitude:", lat)
show("  Longitude:", lon)
show("  Altitude:", alt)

# 4. Swapping Variables
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = [b, a]
show("Swapped -> a:", a, "b:", b)

sections.title: Cardinality Mismatch
sections.content: Attempting to unpack into fewer or more variables than elements in the sequence will trigger a `RunTimeError: Expected N values to unpack, got M`.

arithmetic-ops.title: Arithmetic & Assignment Operators
arithmetic-ops.summary: Full suite of arithmetic calculations, exponentiation, floor division, and augmented assignment operators.

sections.title: Mathematical Operators
sections.content:
Sardine implements standard mathematical operations following algebraic operator precedence rules: parentheses, exponentiation, unary signs, multiplicative operations, and additive operations.

All arithmetic operators support compound/augmented assignment (e.g. `+=`, `**=`).

comparison-logical.title: Comparison & Logical Operators
comparison-logical.summary: Relational comparisons, equality tests, short-circuit logical boolean operators, and precedence rules.

sections.title: Comparison & Logical Precedence
sections.content:
Sardine provides relational operators that return boolean values `True` (1) or `False` (0).

Logical operators use the keywords `not`, `and`, and `or` with strict precedence:
1. `not` (highest)
2. `and`
3. `or` (lowest)

Logical evaluation uses short-circuit semantics: in `A and B`, `B` is not evaluated if `A` is falsy. In `A or B`, `B` is not evaluated if `A` is truthy.

sections.title: Operators Overview
sections.content:
# Relational
==  !=  <  >  <=  >=

# Logical
not expr
expr1 and expr2
expr1 or expr2

sections.title: Evaluations & Precedence
sections.code:
x = 10
y = 20
z = 30

show("x < y:", x < y)
show("x == y:", x == y)
show("x != y:", x != y)
show("y <= 20:", y <= 20)

# Logical Combinations
show("(x < y) and (y < z):", (x < y) and (y < z))
show("(x > y) or (y < z):", (x > y) or (y < z))
show("not (x == 10):", not (x == 10))

# Precedence: not > and > or
# (1 and 0) or (not 0) -> 0 or 1 -> 1 (True)
result = (1 and 0) or not 0
show("Precedence check (1 and 0) or not 0:", result)

bitwise-ops.title: Bitwise Operations
bitwise-ops.summary: Direct bit-manipulation operators: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, left-shift, and right-shift.

sections.title: Bitwise Manipulation
sections.content:
Sardine executes bitwise operations natively on 64-bit integer values using native C++ bitwise semantics. Bitwise operators include bitwise AND (`&`), bitwise OR (`|`), bitwise XOR (`^`), bitwise invert (`~`), left-shift (`<<`), and right-shift (`>>`).

Each operator also has a compound assignment variant: `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`.

sections.title: Bitwise Gates & Masks
sections.code:
a = 12   # Binary: 1100
b = 10   # Binary: 1010

show("a & b (AND):", a & b)      # 1000 = 8
show("a | b (OR):", a | b)       # 1110 = 14
show("a ^ b (XOR):", a ^ b)      # 0110 = 6
show("~a (Bitwise NOT):", ~a)    # -13

# Shifts
x = 1
show("1 << 4 (Left Shift):", x << 4)    # 16
show("16 >> 2 (Right Shift):", 16 >> 2) # 4

# Compound Bitwise Assignment
mask = 1
mask <<= 3
show("mask <<= 3:", mask)

ternary-expr.title: Ternary Conditional Expression
ternary-expr.summary: Compact inline conditional expressions using the `? :` operator.

sections.title: Inline Decision Making
sections.content: The ternary operator `condition ? true_val : false_val` allows conditional logic to be written inline within an expression. It evaluates the condition first; if truthy, it returns the true branch value, otherwise the false branch value.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
sections.content: result = condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false

sections.title: Ternary Assignments & Nesting
sections.code:
score = 85
status = score >= 50 ? "PASSED" : "FAILED"
show("Exam status:", status)

# Inline string construction
age = 17
access = $"User is {age >= 18 ? 'an Adult' : 'a Minor'}"
show(access)

# Chained / Nested Ternary
val = 0
sign = val > 0 ? "Positive" : (val < 0 ? "Negative" : "Zero")
show("Sign of", val, "is", sign)

sections.content:

Sign of 0 is Zero

sections.title: Conditionals in Sardine
sections.content:
Instead of traditional keywords, Sardine uses natural, declarative keywords for branching:
* `when <condition> { ... }`: Evaluates condition; if truthy, executes the block.
* `orwhen <condition> { ... }`: Optional subsequent condition if preceding checks were falsy.
* `otherwise { ... }`: Default fallback block executed if no prior branch was taken.

**Truthiness Rules**:
* Falsy values: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `Null`, `None`, `null`, `False`.
* Truthy values: All non-zero numbers, non-empty strings, populated lists/dictionaries, and `True`.

menu-switch.title: Menu / Choice / Fallback (Switch-Case)
menu-switch.summary: Multi-way branch matching with expression evaluation, fall-through execution, and escape break.

sections.title: Menu Switch Constructs
sections.content:
The `menu` construct in Sardine matches an expression against several `choice` branches with a default `fallback` path.

**Fall-Through Execution**: Like C/C++ switch statements, Sardine's `choice` blocks execute subsequent branches upon matching *unless* an explicit `escape` keyword is invoked to break out of the menu.

sections.content: If you do not want subsequent `choice` blocks to run after a match, always include an `escape` statement at the end of the choice body.

cycle-loop.title: Cycle Loop (For Loop)
cycle-loop.summary: Range-based step iteration with start, stop, and step increments, featuring zero-allocation in-place scoping.

sections.title: Numeric Range Iteration
sections.content:
The `cycle` loop provides high-performance numeric range iteration equivalent to a traditional C/Python `for` loop. It supports start, stop (inclusive), and step values.

Under the hood, Sardine reuses frame environments and bypasses dynamic result accumulation during cycle loops, keeping memory consumption completely flat even over millions of iterations.

during-loop.title: During Loop (While Loop)
during-loop.summary: Condition-driven while loop construct evaluated before every iteration cycle.

sections.title: Condition-Driven Loops
sections.content: The `during` construct executes its block repeatedly as long as its conditional expression resolves to truthy. The condition is re-evaluated before each iteration cycle.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
Dynamic State Evaluation with During

# Accumulating values until threshold
total = 0
counter = 1

during counter <= 5 {
    total += counter
    show($"Added {counter}, Running total = {total}")
    counter += 1
}

show("Final Sum:", total)

# Binary Halving
val = 64
steps = 0
during val > 1 {
    val //= 2
    steps += 1
}
show("Halved 64 to 1 in", steps, "steps")

sections.title: Sandbox Limit
sections.content: By default, the execution sandbox intercepts loops exceeding 100,000 iterations to protect against accidental infinite loops. Pass `--unbounded` if you require longer iterations.

trace-loop.summary: Collection-driven foreach iteration over lists, strings, and multi-variable pair unpacking.

sections.title: Collection Traversal with Trace
sections.content:
The `trace` loop is Sardine's foreach construct. It iterates over any sequence using the `<-` assignment arrow.

`trace` can iterate directly over lists, characters of a string, or unroll nested pairs/tuples into multiple variables (e.g. `trace k, v <- pairs`).

loop-control.title: Loop Jump Controls (Proceed & Escape)
loop-control.summary: Interrupt loop execution using `proceed` (continue to next cycle) and `escape` (break out of loop).

sections.title: Proceed and Escape
sections.content:
Sardine provides two explicit jump keywords for loop flow:
* `proceed`: Skips the remainder of the current iteration and jumps directly to the next iteration (equivalent to `continue` in C/Python).
* `escape`: Terminates the innermost loop immediately and transfers control to the statement after the loop (equivalent to `break` in C/Python).

functions.title: Method Declarations (Functions)
functions.summary: Declaring named functions using the `method` keyword, parameter passing, and invocation.

sections.title: First-Class Functions
sections.content:
Functions in Sardine are first-class citizens declared with the `method` keyword. Functions can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned from functions.

Function parameters are bound into a newly allocated execution scope with access to parent scopes.

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
Defining & Invoking Functions
sections.code:
# Basic method definition
method greet(name) {
    yield $"Hello, {name}! Welcome to Sardine."

yield-return.title: Yield & Return Values
yield-return.summary: Returning values using `yield`, implicit Null returns, and multi-value returns.

sections.title: Yield Semantics
sections.content:
In Sardine, `yield` acts as the return statement of a function, immediately passing control and a result value back to the caller.

* **Implicit Null**: If a function terminates without an explicit `yield` or calls a bare `yield`, it returns `Null`.
* **Multiple Returns**: `yield val1, val2, val3` returns multiple values packaged as a list, which can be destructured on the caller side.

sections.title: List Data Structure
sections.content:
Lists in Sardine are dynamic, heterogeneous ordered sequences declared with square brackets `[...]`. Elements can be accessed and modified by 0-based index.

**Copy-on-Write (COW)**: Sardine uses Copy-on-Write semantics for lists. Passing or returning a list shares internal memory until a mutating method modifies the contents.

list-comprehensions.title: List Comprehensions
list-comprehensions.summary: Expressive syntactic constructs to generate transformed and filtered lists using `cycle` and `trace`.

sections.title: Comprehension Forms
sections.content:
Sardine supports concise list comprehensions combining an expression with either a `cycle` or `trace` clause and an optional `when` filter condition:

1. **Cycle Comprehension**: `[expr cycle i = start:end (:step)? (when cond)?]`
2. **Trace Comprehension**: `[expr trace item <- collection (when cond)?]`
3. **Multi-Variable Trace Comprehension**: `[expr trace k, v <- pairs (when cond)?]`

sections.title: Syntax Blueprint
sections.content:
# Range-based with filter
[x ** 2 cycle x = 1 : 10 when x % 2 == 0]

# Sequence-based with filter
[item.upper() trace item <- words when len(item) > 3]

sections.title: Generating Transformed Lists
sections.code:
# 1. Squares of numbers 1 to 5
squares = [x * x cycle x = 1 : 5]
show("Squares:", squares)

# 2. Filtered even numbers from 0 to 10 with step
evens = [n cycle n = 0 : 10 : 2]
show("Evens (step 2):", evens)

# 3. Squares of odd numbers with 'when' clause
odd_squares = [x ** 2 cycle x = 1 : 10 when x % 2 != 0]
show("Odd squares:", odd_squares)

# 4. Transforming an existing list via trace
raw_names = ["alice", "bob", "charlie", "dan"]
uppers = [name.upper() trace name <- raw_names when len(name) > 3]
show("Filtered Uppercase names:", uppers)

# 5. Extracting and calculating from pairs
pairs = [[1, 10], [2, 20], [3, 30]]
sums = [k + v trace k, v <- pairs]
show("Pair sums:", sums)

sections.title: Comprehension Scope Isolation
sections.content: Variables defined inside a comprehension clause (like `x` in `cycle x = 1:5`) are scoped strictly to the comprehension and do not overwrite variables in the enclosing environment.

dictionaries.title: Dictionaries (Hash Maps)
dictionaries.summary: Key-value hash maps, indexing, dictionary merging, and key dropping operations.

sections.title: Dictionary Fundamentals
sections.content:
Dictionaries in Sardine store key-value mappings inside `{key: value, ...}`. Keys can be strings or numbers. Values can be any data type, including nested lists, models, or other dictionaries.

Sardine features dedicated operators for dictionaries:
* `+`: Merges two dictionaries. If duplicate keys exist, RHS overwrites LHS.
* `-`: Removes a key from a dictionary (e.g. `dict - "key"`).

sections.content:
d = {"host": "localhost", "port": 8080}
value = d["host"]       # Direct access
d["port"] = 9000        # Mutation
merged = d1 + d2        # Merges d1 and d2
dropped = d - "host"    # Removes key

model-definition.summary: Declaring object blueprints using the `model` keyword, member methods, and object instantiation.

sections.title: Object-Oriented Programming with Models
sections.content:
In Sardine, classes are defined using the `model` keyword. Models encapsulate state (attributes) and behavior (methods).

Instances of a model are instantiated by calling the model name like a function: `instance = ModelName(arguments)`.

sections.title: Access Control Specifiers
sections.content:
Sardine enforces strict encapsulation with three visibility modifiers that can be applied to both attributes (`attr <...>`) and methods (`method ...()`):

* `open`: **Public**. Unrestricted access from anywhere, including external callers.
* `guarded`: **Protected**. Accessible within the defining model and all derived subclasses.
* `secret`: **Private**. Strictly restricted to the defining model. Subclasses and external callers cannot read or modify secret members.

constructors.title: Constructors & Initializers (`init`)
constructors.summary: Named `init` constructors with C++-style initializer lists, default parameters, and execution bodies.

sections.title: Constructor Architecture
sections.content:
Constructors in Sardine are named `init`. They feature a dedicated **initializer list** section before the constructor body, setting attributes before body execution begins.

Parameters can specify default values. Resolved member offsets are cached in the C++ engine for fast O(1) attribute setup.

model DatabaseConfig {
    open attr <host, port, username, max_connections>

    init(host = "localhost", port = 5432, username = "postgres", max_connections = 100) {
        host: host,
        port: port,
        username: username,
        max_connections: max_connections
        show($"Config created: {username}@{host}:{port} (Pool: {max_connections})")
    }
}

# 1. Using default parameters
cfg1 = DatabaseConfig()

# 2. Overriding port and host positionally
cfg2 = DatabaseConfig("db.production.internal", 5433)

# 3. Custom user and connections
cfg3 = DatabaseConfig("10.0.0.5", 5432, "app_user", 500)

* **Late-binding**: Overridden methods are dispatched dynamically based on the concrete instance at runtime.

type-reflection.title: Type Checking (`is_a` & `type`)
type-reflection.summary: Runtime type reflection, polymorphic instance checks, and type identity.

sections.title: Runtime Type Inspection
sections.content:
Sardine provides two primary built-ins for type inspection:
* `type(val)`: Returns the string type name (e.g. `'Integer'`, `'String'`, `'List'`, or the model name).
* `is_a(instance, ModelClass)`: Tests if an object is an instance of a given model class or any of its parent classes in the inheritance hierarchy.

show("type('text'):", type("text"))

# Testing is_a() hierarchy

show("is_a(c, Shape):", is_a(c, Shape))
show("is_a(c, Rectangle):", is_a(c, Rectangle))
show("is_a(r, Shape):", is_a(r, Shape))

sections.title: Exception Interception
sections.content:
Sardine replaces traditional try-catch-finally keywords with declarative keywords:
* `risk { ... }`: The protected code block where potential exceptions may occur.
* `trap [ErrorType] [err_var] { ... }`: Catches specified or generic errors. Captured error objects expose `.message` and `.traceback`.
* `clean { ... }`: Cleanup block that is **always guaranteed to execute**, regardless of whether an exception was thrown.

# 1. Write CSV file using CSVWriter
writer = csv.CSVWriter("employees.csv")
writer.write_row(["id", "name", "role", "salary"])
writer.write_row([101, "Souvik", "Engineer", 95000])
writer.write_row([102, "Diptoneel", "Architect", 105000])
writer.write_row([103, "Arkopravo", "Lead", 110000])
writer.close()

# 2. Read back using CSVReader
reader = csv.CSVReader("employees.csv")
show("Detected Headers:", reader.headers)

# Read row as list
row1 = reader.read_row()
show("Row 1 list:", row1)

# Read row mapped to headers as Dictionary
row2_dict = reader.read_dict_row()
show("Row 2 dict:", row2_dict)
show("Row 2 name:", row2_dict["name"], "| salary:", row2_dict["salary"])

reader.close()

sandboxing.title: Runtime Safeguards & Sandboxing
sandboxing.summary: Protective resource thresholds, stack depth limits, AST limits, and runtime performance optimizations.

sections.title: Execution Safeguards
sections.content: To prevent browser freezing, memory leaks, and runaway recursive loops, Sardine incorporates hard thresholds enforced at runtime.

sections.title: Sandbox Boundaries
rows: Limits cycles, while conditions, and comprehensions from freezing.
Prevents recursive stack overflows from exhausting thread memory.
Halts deeply recursive syntactic nesting during Pratt parsing.
Prevents heap exhaustion through runaway sequence allocation.
Restricts file stream memory consumption in local mode.

sections.title: C++23 Optimization Pillars
sections.content:
Sardine achieves native-grade execution speeds while retaining dynamic scripting flexibility through key design decisions in the engine:

* **Copy-on-Write (COW) Containers**: Lists and Dictionaries defer deep copying until write operations occur.
* **Static AST Dispatch (RTTI Elimination)**: The recursive evaluator evaluates nodes using static numeric enums rather than expensive C++ `dynamic_cast` lookups.
* **Thread-Local Object Pool**: Numbers are allocated from a dedicated thread-local memory pool, bypassing standard heap fragmentation.
* **Pointer-Keyed String Interning**: Interns variable identifiers and dictionary keys for O(1) pointer-equality comparisons.
* **Resolved Member Caching**: Caches constructor entry points and polymorphic method offsets inside models for constant-time dispatch.

./build/sardine production_script.sad --unbounded
